paragraphs: A) In the Mishnah: Orlah 2:12; Rosh Hashanah 2:5; Yevamot 16:7; Sotah 9:15; Gittin 4:2, 3; Avot 1:16. (See Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel the Elder.)

B) Rabban Gamliel the Elder—he is the unqualified “Rabban Gamliel”—son of Rabban Shimon, son of Hillel the Elder. He was the first among the prophets [בנביאים] to be called Rabban; so writes the Arukh, entry Abaye. Thus Yuchasin erred in writing “son of Rabbi Shimon.” See Asarah Maamarot, treatise Chikkur Din, part 2, chapter 19, for the reason he was called Rabban even though “his name” is greater than Rabban; see there in the Yad Yehudah commentary, section 34. See the translator’s introduction to Maimonides’ commentary on the Mishnah, order Nashim, and you will see that there is an error there.

C) Yuchasin writes [in the order of the generations]: “Even while the Temple stood, Rabban Gamliel the Elder was in Yavneh, although he was in Jerusalem, for the Sanhedrin went into exile forty years before the destruction; there Shmuel HaKatan instituted the blessing concerning the sectarians before him. Rashi writes, Rosh Hashanah 31, beginning of side b, that Rabban Gamliel the Elder was in Usha and returned to Yavneh; so it appears. But what Rashi writes, that his son Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel”—meaning, Shimon the martyr, son of Rabban Gamliel the Elder—“returned to Usha, as he writes in the last chapter of Rosh Hashanah, is not so. For the Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel mentioned there, 32a, who was in Usha, is Shimon, son of Gamliel of Yavneh, Rabbi’s father, as is clearly apparent from the sages who spoke with him: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka”—in the reading before us Rabbi Yishmael is not mentioned, only Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka—“and Rabbi Chanina, son of Rabbi Yose HaGelili, who were after Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri disagreed with Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh about sanctifying the month. Thus what Rashi writes, that Shimon the martyr, son of Rabban Gamliel the Elder, returned to Usha, is not so; rather, Shimon, son of Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh, was in Usha. For Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asked the emperor for Yavneh and its sages, that he should not kill them. From this it appears that before the destruction he was in Yavneh; Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh were there too. But Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel of Yavneh, Rabbi’s father, was in Usha.” End of the quotation from Yuchasin. His objection to Rashi, of blessed memory, is puzzling. At 31, beginning of side b, s.v. “In Yavneh in the days of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai; Usha in the days of Rabban Gamliel the Elder; and he returned to Yavneh”—the reading in Ein Yaakov misled him. Likewise, in Shalshelet HaKabbalah, 32, end of side b, the reading is “Usha in the days of Rabban Gamliel the Elder.” But the reading before us is correct: “Usha in the days of Rabban Gamliel”—meaning Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh, father of Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi’s father—“and they returned from Usha to Yavneh; in the days of his son Rabbi Shimon”—he is Rabbi’s father—“they returned to Usha, as is taught below in our chapter, 32a: ‘When the court sanctified …’” This means the passage there: “When the court sanctified the year in Usha, Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka went down before the ark …, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said to him, ‘This is how they used to act in Yavneh.’” Rashi explains: “In my father’s days, when the Sanhedrin was there.” End of quotation. See Niddah 14b: Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok asked the sages in Usha; there, 48b: he said, “This is how they used to explain in Yavneh.” In the Jerusalem Talmud, end of Sanhedrin chapter 1, Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok said, “When Rabban Gamliel was sitting in court in Yavneh, my father sat at his right.” In Rashi, end of chapter Bakhol Mearvin: Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok was in the time of Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh, Rabbi Yehoshua’s disputant. In Usha they enacted ordinances: Ketubbot 49b; Rashi, Bava Metzia 35, end of side a. See above, Rabbi Yishmael, who was among those who went to Usha. All the foregoing thus proves that Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh, grandson of Rabban Gamliel the Elder, was in Usha and returned to Yavneh, and in the days of his son Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi’s father, they returned to Usha. This also follows from Rashi’s own wording: “Yavneh in the days of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai; Usha in the days of Rabban Gamliel”—that is, Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh. Had he meant Rabban Gamliel the Elder, he should have put him first, since Rabban Gamliel the Elder was patriarch and died eighteen years before the destruction, whereas Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai became patriarch after the destruction, after Shimon’s killing, for only two and a half years (see his entry). Thus in Rabban Gamliel the Elder’s days they were not yet in Usha. This also follows from the question raised in the Jerusalem Talmud, Peah, beginning of chapter 1: Rabbi Yeshvav distributed his property, and Rabban Gamliel the Elder sent to him, “Did they not say”—in Usha—“that one who gives away lavishly should not give away more than one fifth?” It asks, “But Rabban Gamliel preceded Usha”—meaning, how could he send them the ordinances of Usha when he preceded Usha? It answers, “They had this law”—meaning, before they enacted it in Usha—“and forgot it; the later ones arose”—meaning, in Usha—“and agreed with the view of the earlier ones.” End of quotation. Long afterwards, the newly printed second Sefer Ir Binyamin came into my hands. In tractate Peah it writes as follows: “I was greatly astonished by the Jerusalem Talmud’s question here, ‘Rabban Gamliel preceded Usha.’ Does not Rosh Hashanah count, among those ten exiles of the Sanhedrin, from Yavneh to Usha, from Usha to Yavneh, and from Yavneh to Usha? Rashi explains: ‘Yavneh in the days of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai; Usha in the days of Rabban Gamliel the Elder,’ and there that ordinance was enacted”—meaning, the ordinance of Usha was thus in Rabban Gamliel the Elder’s days; how, then, could it ask that Rabban Gamliel the Elder preceded the ordinance of Usha? He writes: “Unless we say that it was clear to the Jerusalem Talmud that this Rabban Gamliel, who sent to Rabbi Yeshvav, preceded the ordinance of Usha, because this ordinance was enacted when they went into exile to Usha the second time, which was after Rabban Gamliel the Elder.” End of quotation. He too encountered the erroneous reading in Rashi, “Usha in the days of Rabban Gamliel the Elder,” as in the Ein Yaakov reading. Thus his attempt to answer the Jerusalem Talmud’s difficulty by saying that this ordinance was enacted when they went into exile to Usha the second time is also incorrect. In my opinion, of the ten exiles, their exile from the Chamber of Hewn Stone to the shops, from the shops to Jerusalem, and from Jerusalem to Yavneh occurred in the forty years before the destruction. Their exile from Yavneh to Usha and so forth occurred after the destruction. It likewise appears that Rabban Gamliel the Elder was in Yavneh before the destruction, for Shmuel HaKatan, who died in his lifetime, instituted the blessing concerning the sectarians before him in Yavneh; Rabban Gamliel the Elder died eighteen years before the destruction. (See above, Rabbi Eliezer ben Horkenos: a heavenly voice came forth in an upper room in Yavneh, saying that the Divine Presence and the holy spirit were fit to rest upon two, and they directed their eyes toward Shmuel HaKatan.) It is possible that they also went into exile to Usha before the destruction, in the days of Shimon the martyr; but their second exile to Yavneh and their second to Usha were in the days of Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh and his son Rabbi Shimon. (See Chananya, deputy of the priests, where I wrote in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud, Pesachim, that he preceded Usha and was killed at the destruction; thus they were not in Usha before the destruction.) Accordingly, as for Rosh Hashanah chapter 4, folio 31: “The Sanhedrin underwent ten exiles: from the Chamber of Hewn Stone to the shops, to Jerusalem, to Yavneh, to Usha, to Yavneh, to Usha, to Shefaram, to Beit Shearim, to Tzippori, to Tiberias”—one may say that before the destruction they went into exile from Jerusalem to Yavneh, where Rabban Gamliel the Elder was, and its period of residence there continued into the days of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. In Rosh Hashanah 29b: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted an ordinance after the destruction; Rabbi Elazar said, “He enacted it only in Yavneh.” Thus they were in Yavneh after the destruction. They went into exile to Usha in the days of Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh, and in his days returned from Usha to Yavneh. In the days of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi’s father, they returned to Usha, as Rashi writes; and in Rabbi’s days, to Beit Shearim, Tzippori, and Tiberias, as Rashi writes. Thus Yuchasin, Shalshelet HaKabbalah, the author of Ir Binyamin, and the author of Ein Yaakov all erred and were mistaken about what lay before them.

D) Rabban Gamliel the Elder enacted ordinances: Eruvin 45a; Gittin 32a, 34b. Yuchasin writes [under Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh]: “In Tosefta Shabbat, chapter 7: one burns objects in honor of patriarchs as one does in honor of kings. When Rabban Gamliel the Elder died, Onkelos (see his entry) burned his bed and the articles he used, worth seventy Tyrian maneh: Avodah Zarah 11a. Each maneh is twenty-five shekels. Some explain seventy maneh as seventy times one hundred, which is seven thousand dinars. He waived his own dignity, and they brought him out in linen garments: Ketubbot 8b; Moed Katan 27b.” End of quotation. When he died, the honor of Torah ceased: end of Sotah, 49a. The Arukh, entry batel—a scribal error; it should read entry kavod—explains: people who honor Torah scholars. In chapter Hakore et HaMegillah, 21a: until Rabban Gamliel the Elder they would study Torah standing; when he died, illness descended upon the world and they studied sitting. This is what we learned: “When Rabban Gamliel the Elder died, the honor of Torah ceased, and purity and abstinence died” (Mishnah, chapter Eglah Arufah). He was among the Men of the Great Assembly (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1).

E) Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua were present at his death, and also at the death of his grandson Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh, and ruled concerning overturning his bed: Moed Katan 27a. Belorit the female convert asked Rabban Gamliel …; Rabbi Yose the priest took up her question: Rosh Hashanah 17b. This requires examination, for it appears that this Rabban Gamliel, with Rabbi Yosef the priest, who was a student of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, is Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh. Agrippas, a military commander—he was a Roman appointed over the heads of the troops, and lived in the time of King Agrippas; Rashi—asked Rabban Gamliel: Avodah Zarah 55a. Shimon HaPakuli arranged the eighteen blessings before him (see his entry). Shimon the martyr and Yoezer of the Birah asked him. Rabbi Shimon ben Netanel was his son-in-law. Shmuel HaKatan went up to intercalate years. He eulogized Shmuel HaKatan (see his entry). Chizkiyah, father of Ikkesh, testified before him. Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa prayed for his son. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was his colleague. Nechemyah of Beit Deli received a tradition from him. Shimon of Mitzpah was before him.
